articles.title: WHO – with support from Italy – brings health care closer to families in eastern Afghanistan
articles.description: Countries: Afghanistan, Italy Source: World Health Organization 30 August 2026, Kabul, Afghanistan – With financial support from the Government of Italy, the World Health Organization (WHO) is bringing essential primary health care services to families living in remote communities in Afghanistan. At Gari Basic Health Centre, this support helps health workers provide timely treatment, follow-up care and essential health advice to people who might otherwise struggle to access care. Mohammad’s family lives in Mani village, more than 90 minutes on foot from the nearest health facility. When 14-month-old Mohammad sustained a severe burn on his leg that left him unable to walk, his parents were concerned that the wound would become infected before they had time to access appropriate care. “We were very worried because my child’s leg was badly burned and we live so far from the health centre,” said Rayees, Mohammad’s father. The family brought Mohammad to Gari Basic Health Centre, supported by WHO through a primary health care project funded by the Government of Italy, where health workers immediately assessed his wound and applied dressings. They comforted his parents and showed them how to care for the injury and prevent infection at home. Follow-up visits were scheduled every 2 days to monitor Mohammad’s recovery. “Thanks to the care we received at the health centre, my son recovered completely,” said Rayees. “We are grateful to the health workers for their care and kindness, and we thank WHO for bringing these essential services closer to our community.” “Access to quality primary health care is essential to protect the health and well-being of communities, particularly in remote areas where distance can delay treatment and turn manageable conditions into serious complications,” said WHO Representative in Afghanistan Dr Edwin Ceniza Salvador. “With support from the Government of Italy, WHO and its partners are strengthening frontline health services and bringing timely care closer to underserved communities. This contribution helps reduce health inequities and ensure that more people can receive essential services when needed.” For families in remote communities, continued donor support can mean the difference between delayed treatment and timely care. For Mohammad’s family, Italy’s contribution meant a full recovery and the reassurance that help was within reach. WHO thanks the Government of Italy for its valuable contribution and acknowledges health partners and frontline health workers who turn this support into essential care for communities across Afghanistan.

articles.title: Baby Goats With Rabies Spark Petting Zoo Panic
articles.description: MediaNews Group/Boulder Daily Ca / David Jennings, Getty Images North Carolina health officials are warning visitors to a mobile petting zoo that some of the animals they came into contact with may have had rabies. Three baby goats from Farm Adventures have tested positive for rabies and a fourth was assumed to be infected. People who visited the mobile petting zoo’s location in Harmony or at off-site events between July 28 and August 27 are at risk of having been exposed. Health officials listed 10 events where people may have been exposed, including one at an assisted-living facility and a back-to-school party. “There is not a broad risk to the public—only those who attended events at the mobile petting zoo and were in close contact with the goats are at risk,” officials said. The health department said the outbreak most likely came from a skunk that had entered the goats’ pen in late July. “Residents should not wait for symptoms before calling,” Mecklenburg County Health Director Kimberly Scott said. Farm Adventures said its “4 precious baby goats” were euthanized and its staff is “closely monitoring our remaining animals under the guidelines provided by health officials.” Read it at CNN Read more at The Daily Beast.
